newsitem.title: USA: U.S. 10-year notes receive lukewarm reception.
newsitem.headline: U.S. 10-year notes receive lukewarm reception.

text.p: For the second straight day, the U.S. Treasury market gave a lukewarm reception to new supply, making players nervous over prospects for the final leg of the refunding on Thursday.
Wednesday, the Treasury sold $10 billion 10-year notes at an average yield of 6.273 percent, in line with expectations.

"It came in around what we were looking for; there were no real surprises," said Bill Kan, money market economist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc. "Given the recent (economic and political news) the levels were about right."
Noncompetitive bids were $306 million, lower than the recent 10-year note average of around $400 million, but slightly above the $284 million seen in the prior 10-year sale.
And at 2.41 the bid to cover ratio was a bit better than the prior two auctions and above most 10-year auctions this year, analysts noted.

"It was a difficult auction; we tried to take it on the high of the recent move (upward)," said Brett Benza, senior trader at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, adding the auction was mostly dealer-driven.

"The Street was forced into underwriting (the supply) at more expensive levels than they wanted to," Benza said. "Retail customers who pushed the market up (the past few sessions) did not show up after the auction. That makes the bond auction all the more interesting tomorrow."
Since the auction, the when-issued 10-year note has sunk almost three basis points to 6.30 percent.
One trader said that the market tried to build in concessions, but when a large hedge fund started buying the when-issued notes earlier, the market "got scared," and pushed down the yield.
The 10-year note sale comes on the heels of a weak three-year note auction Tuesday. But in contrast, the three-year traded at a profit after the auction.

The market now looks ahead to Thursday's 30-year bond auction. Players said they hope to buy the bond no more expensive than 6.60 percent. The when-issued 30-year is now at 6.57. Traders were hopeful the auction will go better than the prior two.
"They could go OK at these levels," a trader said. "But the only thing bonds are cheap to are 10-years."
